title: UNIT 9: STATISTICS & PROBABILITY
notes:
Statistics → The science of collecting, organizing, presenting, analyzing and interpreting data.

Probability → A numerical measure of how likely an event is to occur.

title: 9.1 STATISTICAL DATA
notes:
Statistical data → Information collected for analysis and decision-making.

Statistics helps us:
• Describe the present
• Understand the past
• Estimate or predict the future

title: TYPES OF DATA
notes:
Qualitative data → Non-numerical characteristics.
Example: color, gender, town.

Quantitative data → Numerical information.
Example: age, height, weight, exam score.

Continuous data → Measured values that can take many possible values.
Example: height, temperature.

Discrete data → Counted values, usually whole numbers.
Example: number of students.

title: DATA COLLECTION
notes:
Primary data → Collected directly by the researcher.
Examples: surveys, interviews, experiments and observations.

Secondary data → Obtained from existing sources.
Examples: government records, school records and institutional reports.

Common methods:
• Interview
• Observation
• Questionnaire
• Experiment

title: POPULATION & SAMPLE
notes:
Population → The complete collection of individuals, objects or measurements being studied.

Sample → A subset selected from the population.

A sample is useful when studying the entire population is:
• Difficult
• Expensive
• Time-consuming
• Impractical

title: DESCRIPTIVE & INFERENTIAL STATISTICS
notes:
Descriptive statistics → Organizes, summarizes and describes collected data.

Inferential statistics → Uses sample data to make conclusions about a larger population.

Easy way to remember:
DESCRIBE → What does the data show?
INFER → What can we conclude about the population?

title: TABULATION & FREQUENCY DISTRIBUTION
notes:
Tabulation → Systematic presentation of data using rows and columns.

Frequency → The number of times a value occurs.

Frequency distribution → Shows values or class intervals together with their frequencies.

Raw data → Data that has not yet been organized.

title: GRAPHICAL PRESENTATION
notes:
Graphs make data easier to compare, analyze and interpret.

Common statistical graphs:
• Bar chart
• Dual bar chart
• Pie chart
• Histogram

title: PIE CHART
notes:
A pie chart is a circle divided into sectors.

Sector size is proportional to frequency.

FORMULAS
Percentage = (Category frequency ÷ Total frequency) × 100%

Sector angle = (Category frequency ÷ Total frequency) × 360°

Example: If frequency = 20 and total = 100:
Percentage = 20%
Angle = 72°

title: HISTOGRAM
notes:
A histogram represents a frequency distribution.

x-axis → Variable or class intervals
y-axis → Frequency
Bars → Represent class intervals
Bar height → Represents frequency

Unlike a bar chart, histogram bars represent continuous class intervals and touch each other.

title: 9.1.3 MEASURES OF CENTRAL TENDENCY
notes:
Measures of central tendency describe the central or typical value of a dataset.

The three main measures are:

1. Mean
2. Median
3. Mode

title: ARITHMETIC MEAN
notes:
Mean → The sum of all observations divided by the number of observations.

FORMULA
x̄ = Σx ÷ n

For x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ:
x̄ = (x₁ + x₂ + ... + xₙ) ÷ n

For frequency data:
x̄ = Σfx ÷ Σf

Example:
Data: 2, 4, 6
Mean = (2 + 4 + 6) ÷ 3 = 4

title: MEDIAN
notes:
Median → The middle value after arranging data in ascending or descending order.

If n is odd:
Median = Middle observation

If n is even:
Median = Average of the two middle observations

The median is less affected by extreme values than the mean.

title: MODE
notes:
Mode → The value that occurs most frequently.

A dataset can have:
• One mode → Unimodal
• More than one mode → Multimodal
• No mode → No value occurs more frequently

Mode can also be used with categorical data.

title: 9.1.4 MEASURES OF DISPERSION
notes:
Dispersion → Measures how spread out the data values are.

Main measures:
• Range
• Variance
• Standard deviation

Central tendency tells us the CENTER; dispersion tells us the SPREAD.

title: RANGE
notes:
Range → Difference between the largest and smallest values.

FORMULA
Range = Maximum value − Minimum value

Example:
Data: 3, 7, 10, 15
Range = 15 − 3 = 12

title: VARIANCE
notes:
Variance → The mean of the squared deviations from the arithmetic mean.

For individual data:
σ² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ n

For frequency data:
σ² = Σf(x − x̄)² ÷ Σf

Variance measures how far values tend to spread from the mean.

title: STANDARD DEVIATION
notes:
Standard deviation → The square root of variance.

FORMULA
σ = √σ²

Interpretation:
Small σ → Data values are close together.
Large σ → Data values are more spread out.

title: EFFECT OF ADDING A CONSTANT
notes:
If the same constant k is added to every observation:

Mean → Increases by k

Variance → Unchanged

Standard deviation → Unchanged

Example:
If every value increases by 5, the mean increases by 5, but the spread of the data stays the same.

title: 9.2 PROBABILITY
notes:
Probability → Measures the likelihood that an event will occur.

Experimental probability → Found from the results of repeated trials.

Probability always lies between 0 and 1:
0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1

title: EXPERIMENT
notes:
Experiment → A trial in which an observation or outcome is obtained, but the exact outcome cannot be predicted with certainty beforehand.

Examples:
• Tossing a coin
• Rolling a die
• Drawing a card

title: SAMPLE SPACE
notes:
Sample space (S) → The set of ALL possible outcomes of an experiment.

One coin toss:
S = {H, T}

One die roll:
S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}

Remember:
S = All possible outcomes

title: EVENT
notes:
Event (E) → A subset of the sample space.

Example:
When rolling a die:
S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}

Event of getting an even number:
E = {2, 4, 6}

Event = One or more selected outcomes from S.

title: EQUALLY LIKELY OUTCOMES
notes:
Outcomes are equally likely when each outcome has the SAME chance of occurring.

Example:
For a fair coin:
P(H) = P(T) = 1/2

For a fair die:
Each number has probability 1/6.

title: CERTAIN & IMPOSSIBLE EVENTS
notes:
Certain event → Must occur.
P(E) = 1

Impossible event → Cannot occur.
P(E) = 0

Therefore:
0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1

title: PROBABILITY OF AN EVENT
notes:
For equally likely outcomes:

FORMULA
P(E) = n(E) ÷ n(S)

Where:
n(E) → Number of favorable outcomes
n(S) → Total number of outcomes

Range:
0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1

Example:
Probability of getting an even number on a die:
P(E) = 3 ÷ 6 = 1/2

title: EXPERIMENTAL PROBABILITY
notes:
Experimental probability is based on actual results from repeated trials.

FORMULA
Experimental P(E) = Number of times event occurs ÷ Total number of trials

Example:
Heads occurs 6 times in 10 coin tosses.

P(H) = 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6

title: TREE DIAGRAMS
notes:
A tree diagram systematically lists possible outcomes of successive experiments.

Useful for:
• Repeated coin tosses
• Dice experiments
• Combined experiments
• Multi-step probability problems

Each branch represents a possible outcome.

title: UNIT 9: QUICK REVISION FORMULAS
notes:
STATISTICS

Mean → x̄ = Σx ÷ n
Frequency mean → x̄ = Σfx ÷ Σf
Range → Maximum − Minimum
Variance → σ² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ n
Frequency variance → σ² = Σf(x − x̄)² ÷ Σf
Standard deviation → σ = √σ²

DATA PRESENTATION
Percentage → (Frequency ÷ Total) × 100%
Pie angle → (Frequency ÷ Total) × 360°

PROBABILITY
P(E) = n(E) ÷ n(S)
Experimental P(E) = Successful trials ÷ Total trials

ALWAYS REMEMBER
0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1
